transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-30
Start: 15:00 UTC (08:00 PT)
Duration: ~52 mins
Attendees: Laura Chen (Redwood AE), Marco Silva (Redwood SE), Anika Rao (Redwood CSM), Jon Park (Redwood Platform Eng), Priya Sharma (Oakridge SRE), Ethan Cole (Oakridge CTO), Luis Martinez (Oakridge Lead Backend), Meera Patel (Oakridge Security)

Summary (auto): quick recap of outage where a reload storm + mis-routed fallback caused sustained 5xxs for 14mins; discussion centered on root cause, why KV-cache invalidation cascaded, and how to make fallback deterministic with canary + TTL-based evictions.

[00:00] Laura Chen (Redwood AE): ok everyone thanks for joining, we know this was an annoying morning for you, so we'll go through what we think happened, get the action items locked and hand off the runbook. Priya, do you want to start with a one-line summary from oakridge?

[00:12] Priya Sharma (Oakridge SRE): yeah sure. um so from our side, we saw a config push to the model route that triggered a reload on the cluster, that reload caused many in-flight requests to rehydrate the KV cache at the same time and we hit a cascade where latency spiked then 5xxs. The fallback to the older model didn't seem to engage consistently, some requests kept hitting the new route and got errors.

[00:38] Marco Silva (Redwood SE): can I interrupt — when you say reload, was that a full process restart or a hot-reload?

[00:44] Priya: it looked like hot-reloads but with process-level cache resets. so we lost the in-memory KV prefix essentially. the clients that were mid-stream tried to re-prime the cache and we hit memory pressure across pods.

[00:58] Laura: ok so a combination of bursty cache repop and a fallback policy that had conditions tied to error-rate windows rather than absolute failure of route. that matches what we saw in the telemetry. Marco, you pulled traces?

[01:12] Marco: yes I grabbed the trace sample set. in a few of the top incidents the fallback policy threshold was set at 25% 1m error rate, but the errors were more of a short 10–20s spike in very hot paths, so the policy didn’t flip early enough. also there was a canary weight of 10% configured but traffic hashing sent larger sticky sessions to the new variant, which didn't help.

[01:35] Ethan Cole (Oakridge CTO): can you explain the sticky sessions bit again? our traffic should be uniform — why did some sessions go all to the new variant?

[01:41] Marco: sure — the router uses a consistent-hash on user-id for affinity. when you roll a model variant the hashing can concentrate keys if the key space hot-shifts. combined with autoscaler pod churn, the weight didn't evenly distribute. there's also a small bug we observed in the canary weighting where the weight window wasn't honored during rolling restarts.

[02:05] Luis Martinez (Oakridge): and that led to the KV cache rehydration storm?

[02:08] Marco: exactly. when those concentrated keys hit new pods that had empty KV, those pods issued heavy disk and CPU work to reconstitute caches, slowing token generation and causing errors upstream.

[02:22] Meera Patel (Oakridge Security): this incident also touched our compliance teams — they want to be sure that KMS operations and any key rotation didn't contribute. we don't think KMS was involved but we need the audit traces.

[02:34] Anika Rao (Redwood CSM): we'll attach the KMS audit guidance. Marco, are the KMS logs available in the Redwood console export?

[02:40] Marco: yes, but for private deployments KMS logs might be in the customer's KMS. for hosted we've got the action logs; we'll include where to look. we'll put links in the ticket.

[02:55] Priya: a quick note — we were on a limited retention window for request traces, so we only have high-level metrics for some of the earliest minutes. I'll send the IDs we do have.

[03:06] Laura: perfect — that will help us correlate. ok next, let's walk through the immediate mitigations we propose and get a standing runbook for the on-call. Marco?

[03:17] Marco: short term: 1) change fallback trigger to include instantaneous 30s error spikes (sliding window), 2) set canary affinity to session-randomized hashing so no concentrated keys, 3) throttle KV rehydration by limiting concurrent cache fills per pod (soft semaphore), 4) add a short-lived in-process sticky cache backup to avoid full disk reads. We can push a canary config that implements 1+2 in staging for testing.

[03:49] Luis: any perf hit on throttling rehydration? can't have tail latency blow up in other places.

[03:54] Marco: it's a tradeoff — limiting concurrent fills trades a little per-request latency for stability across pods. based on our sims it's small (<5% p95), much better than full-blown 503s.

[04:08] Ethan: what's the timeline to get these mitigations live in prod if we sign off?

[04:12] Marco: canary config + runbook doc in 4 business days, staging dry-run in 7, production can be phased after the dry-run and a scheduled maintenance window. so roughly two weeks end-to-end with an expedited path.

[04:26] Priya: we prefer earlier — can we accelerate to a hotfix for fallback thresholds this week?

[04:31] Marco: yes we can push a threshold hotfix (just change the error window) — low risk — we can do that within 48 hours.

[04:37] Laura: ok action: Marco to push fallback window change as hotfix and notify Priya; Marco to attach the canary config draft by 05-04.

[04:45] [05:00] Jon Park (Redwood Platform): i wanted to highlight another nuance — the load balancer health check timing: during the reloads the health probe TTL was 5s, which allowed flapping. increasing the probe to 15s with a small grace period reduces churn. worth changing in staging before prod.

[05:09] Priya: yes we saw the flapping. we'll tentatively change health probe in staging and measure.

[05:17] Meera: security question — if we change the fallback logic, do we introduce new audit surfaces? we need to make sure SSO/SAML traces and KMS access attempts are logged.

[05:26] Marco: none of the fallback toggles affect KMS directly; they change routing and in-memory behavior. still, we'll add a step in the runbook to export audit traces for any rollback.

[05:36] [08:45] Priya: quick interruption — i have an ops question about the KV cache invalidation: we currently do prefix eviction on config reloads. could we instead do epoch-based lazy invalidation so old prefixes expire naturally?

[05:58] Marco: yes, epoch-based lazy invalidation is safer. it avoids concurrent rehydration storms, but requires you to keep cold prefix state for a short duration which increases memory needs slightly. we can add a config toggle for that behavior in the runtime.

[06:12] Luis: how big is the mem bump?

[06:15] Marco: from our numbers, about +8–12% memory on heavy workloads. again, better than 503s.

[06:22] Priya: ok we can provision quickly.

[06:25] [16:03] Ethan: let's talk about how this affects our decision for dedicated vs hosted. we were evaluating dedicated because of predictability — does this incident change your recommendation?

[06:41] Marco: it depends — dedicated gives you deterministic capacity and fewer noisy neighbors, but the same runtime behaviors (reloads, cache invalidations) exist. the benefit is you can tune the autoscaler more tightly and have isolated KV stores. If your team wants maximum control and can manage the cluster, dedicated reduces blast radius.

[06:59] Priya: but the runbook controls are the same either way.

[07:03] Marco: right — our immediate mitigation works on both. dedicated buys predictability but not a silver bullet.

[07:10] Meera: one more security ask — can Redwood produce a short note about how fallbacks handle encrypted payloads and whether any data touches disk unencrypted during rehydration?

[07:20] Marco: yes, brief: payloads are encrypted at rest with KMS-managed keys; we do not persist plaintext to disk during rehydration. we'll send the note and certificate snippets for your security review.

[07:29] Laura: ok we're nearing the recap. to be explicit: hotfix fallback threshold in 48h, canary config + runbook by 05-04, Oakridge to supply request IDs and short retention logs by 05-02, staging dry-run week of 05-11. Marco will lead the technical items; Anika will own coordination. any objections?

[07:50] Priya: no objections. thanks.

[08:00] [Final 50:00] Laura: thank you all. we'll follow up with the ticket with attachments: telemetry snapshots, sample traces, and the draft runbook. I'll note the dependencies on your export of request IDs. meeting adjourned.

Notes (auto & manual):
- Telemetry: Redwood shows 14 minute degraded interval, peak 5xx at 1.9% of traffic but concentrated on 3 pods.
- Root cause: config reload + immediate prefix eviction => concurrent KV rehydration => CPU/memory pressure => increased token latency => request timeouts => delayed fallback triggering due to windowed error threshold + canary weight concentration.
- Short term mitigations: fallback window hotfix; canary hashing change; limit concurrent cache fills; increase LB health probe TTL; enable epoch-based lazy invalidation toggle in runtime.
- Long term: automated canary rollout with session-randomized hashing; more conservative default fallback thresholds; optional dedicated deployment guidance (autoscaler and KV sizing).

References shared during call:
- Link: runbook draft (will attach in ticket)
- Link: staging dry-run checklist (to be created)
- Link: sample traces (redwood.telemetry/ORK/2026-04-30)

Action items recap (in transcript):
1) Marco Silva - push fallback threshold hotfix (48h) and attach PR + test notes.
2) Marco Silva - draft canary + rollback config and runbook (due 2026-05-04).
3) Priya Sharma - export incident request IDs and send to Redwood (due 2026-05-02).
4) Anika Rao - attach SOC2/KMS integration guidance to ticket (due 2026-05-05).
5) Luis Martinez - run staging dry-run and report (due 2026-05-08).

End of transcript.
